newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African parliament debates school reform.
newsitem.headline: S.African parliament debates school reform.

text.p: South African Education Minister Sibusiso Bengu on Thursday asked parliament to approve a new education law scrapping apartheid-style schooling and introducing compulsory education for black children.
"This measure will touch virtually every household in our land," he said at the start of a sometimes heated debate.
"(It) establishes national, uniform norms and standards for learners and for school organisation, governance and funding."

The bill, which is assured of support from an overwhelming majority when it comes to a vote, scraps the separate white, black, coloured (mixed-race) and Asian education authorities and places all schooling under the control of a single authority.

It promises a phased elimination of the current spending bias towards white children, on whom the state generally spends four times as much as it does on black children, and it introduces a single syllabus for all schools.
Compulsory education, which has applied to whites for decades, will be phased in for blacks over the next 10 years.

"The passage of this bill should be taken as a monument to all those who laid down their lives in the struggle for non-racial education," said parliamentary education committee chairman Blade Nzimande.

The white-led National Party, which segregated education and steered the lion's share of state funding towards whites for almost 50 years, proposed a series of amendments to soften the effect on predominantly white Afrikaans-language schools.
President Nelson Mandela's ruling African National Congress vowed, however, to reject the amendments when voting takes place some time within the next two weeks.
White-separatist Freedom Front leader Constand Viljoen pledged to oppose the bill because it would destroy the culturally based Afrikaner school system.
The bill proposes to give students a voice in the running of schools and outlaws corporal punishment.
Viljoen said Afrikaners did not allow their children a say in crucial matters such as school governance and believed that parents had a right to spank their children.
"This is a bill of revenge. It aims at retribution. It will force Afrikaners to look to (privately funded) independent schools at great cost and with reluctance," he said.
